'''''Gaudium laevigatum''''', commonly known as the '''coast tea tree''',<ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |title=''Leptospermum laevigatum'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/0950f350-b832-4e5d-a719-11d8c420dba8 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Victoria |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> is a species of shrub or small tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern Australia, but has been widely introduced in other places where it is often considered to be a weed. It has thin, rough bark on the older stems, narrow egg-shaped leaves, relatively large white flowers and flat topped fruit that is shed shortly after reaching maturity.

==Description==
''Gaudium laevigatum'' is a bushy shrub or tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|1.5-6|m}} and has thin, rough bark on the older stems. The young stems are covered with silky hairs at first and have a groove near the base of the [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]. The leaves are greyish green, narrow egg-shaped with the narrower end towards the base, {{cvt|15-30|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-10|mm}} wide on a short petiole. The flowers are borne on short side shoots, usually in pairs of different ages, and are usually {{cvt|15-20|mm}} wide. There are many reddish brown [[bract]]s around the flower buds but most fall off as the flower opens. The [[Hypanthium|floral cup]] is mostly [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]], {{cvt|3-4|mm}} long with the upper part expanded. The [[sepal]]s are triangular, about {{cvt|2|mm}} long, the [[petal]]s white, {{cvt|5-8|mm}} long and the [[stamen]]s {{cvt|1.5-2.5|mm}} long. Flowering mainly occurs from August to October and the fruit is a [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|7-8|mm}} wide with the remains of the sepals initially attached. The fruit mostly fall from the plant shortly after reaching maturity.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |title=''Leptospermum laevigatum'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Leptospermum~laevigatum |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref><ref name="Telopea">{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=Joy |title=A revision of the genus ''Leptospermum'' (Myrtaceae) |journal=Telopea |date=1989 |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=372–373|doi=10.7751/telopea19894902 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="ANPSA">{{cite web |title=''Leptospermum laevigatum'' |url=http://anpsa.org.au/l-lae.html |publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia) |access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
This species was first formally described in 1788 by [[Joseph Gaertner]] who gave it the name ''Fabricia laevigata'' and published the description in his book ''[[De Fructibus et Seminibus Plantarum]]''.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Fabricia laevigata''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/462791 |publisher=APNI|access-date=12 April 2020}}</ref> In 1858, [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] assigned it to the ''Leptospermum'' genus as ''L. laevigatum'' in the ''Parliamentary Papers- Votes and Proceedings of the Legislative Assembly''.<ref name=APNI2>{{cite web|title=''Leptospermum laevigatum''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/524798 |publisher=APNI|access-date=30 May 2025}}</ref>

In 2023, [[Peter Gordon Wilson]] transferred Gaertner's ''Fabricia laevigata'' to ''Gaudium'' as ''G. laevigatum'' in the journal ''[[Taxon (journal)|Taxon]]''.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="Taxon">{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Peter G. |last2=Heslewood |first2=Margaret M. |title=Revised taxonomy of the tribe Leptospermeae (Myrtaceae) based on morphological and DNA data |journal=Taxon |date=2023 |volume=72 |issue=3 |pages=550–571 |doi=10.1002/tax.12892 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/tax.12892 |access-date=28 July 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''laevigatum'') is from a Latin word meaning "made smooth" or "having a polished surface".<ref name="Sharr">{{cite book |author=Francis Aubie Sharr |author-link=Francis Aubie Sharr |title=Western Australian Plant Names and their Meanings |date=2019 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, Western Australia |isbn=978-0-9580341-8-0 |page=233}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Gaudium laevigatum'' is native to New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania where it grows in heath, sometimes forest and on coastal dunes and cliffs south from [[Nambucca Heads, New South Wales|Nambucca Heads]] in New South Wales to [[Anglesea, Victoria|Anglesea]] in Victoria and northern Tasmania. It has also been introduced to Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and countries overseas including southern Africa, New Zealand, Hawaii and the [[Central Coast (California)|Central Coast]] of California.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name=weed>{{cite web|url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/leptospermum_laevigatum.htm|title=Fact Sheet Index|access-date=20 August 2018|work=Weeds of Australia|publisher=[[Queensland Government]]}}</ref><ref name="utas">{{cite web |title=''Leptospermum laevigatum'' |url=https://www.utas.edu.au/dicotkey/dicotkey/MYRTS/sLeptospermum_laevigatum.htm |publisher=University of Tasmania |access-date=13 April 2020}}</ref><ref name=FB>{{FloraBase|name=''Gaudium laevigatum''|id=51902}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Coast teatree is salt-resistant, very [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] and is commonly used in amenities plantings and coastal plantings. It has also been planted in [[Western Australia]] where it has become a weed.<ref>{{cite web | author = Australian Weeds Committee | title = Weed Identification - Coastal Tea Tree | publisher = National Weeds Strategy | url = http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=E12 | access-date = 2007-07-18 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060830192310/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=E12 | archive-date = 2006-08-30 }}</ref>

This species has been planted along the Central Coast of California in the United States<ref name=uc>{{cite web|url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?5179,5190,5191|title=Jepson Manual Treatment|access-date=20 August 2018|publisher=Regents of the University of California}}</ref> and on the [[Cape Flats]]<ref name="ARC South Africa">{{cite web
| url = https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Fact%20Sheets%20Library/Leptospermum%20laevigatum.pdf
| title = Australian myrtle (''Leptospermum laevigatum'')
| publisher = Agricultural Research Centre, South Africa
| series = ARC-PPRI Fact Sheets on invasive plants and their control in South Africa
| access-date = 2024-11-14
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20240723232218/https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Fact%20Sheets%20Library/Leptospermum%20laevigatum.pdf
| archive-date = 2024-07-23
}}</ref> in [[Cape Town]], [[South Africa]], to stabilize [[sand]]. It is known in the United States as the '''Australian tea tree'''<ref name=usda>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=LELA29|title=''Leptospermum laevigatum'' (Sol. ex Gaertn.) F. Muell. Australian teatree |access-date=20 August 2018|publisher=[[USDA]]}}</ref> and in South Africa as the '''Australian myrtle'''.<ref name="ARC South Africa"/> The seeds can be dispersed by wind and water.<ref name=weed/>

It has now become naturalised in [[New Zealand]], southern [[Africa]], [[California]] and [[Hawaii]].<ref name=weed/>

The larvae of ''[[Holocola thalassinana]]'' feed on ''Leptospermum laevigatum''.<ref>{{cite web | author = tortricid.net | title = Holocola | url= http://www.tortricidae.com/catalogueSpeciesList.asp?gcode=486}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
This species is planted widely (as ''Leptospermum laevigatum'') as a garden ornamental or display tree. It is useful as a [[windbreak]] or hedging plant and for the rapid stabilisation of sandy soils, and in rehabilitation areas where construction or mining has taken place.<ref name="weed" /> It has begun to be cultivated for essential oil production, marketed as Coastal tree tree oil, and has shown some beneficial anti-microbial properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Strub |first1=Daniel |title=In-vitro antimicrobial activity of essential oils of Tasmania |journal=Journal of Essential Oil Research |date=28 August 2023 |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=500–508 |doi=10.1080/10412905.2023.2252416 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10412905.2023.2252416 |access-date=21 July 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Conservation status==
''Gaudium laevigatum'' is not listed on the advisory list of rare or threatened plants in Victoria (2014).<ref>{{cite book |title=Advisory list of rare or threatened plants in Victoria |publisher=Department of the Environment and Primary Industries |isbn=978-1-74146-313-2 |url=https://environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0021/50448/Advisory-List-of-Rare-or-Threatened-Plants-in-Victoria-2014.pdf |access-date=5 May 2020}}</ref>
